newsitem.title: USA: FAA suppressed report on ValuJet problems - official.
newsitem.headline: FAA suppressed report on ValuJet problems - official.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration suppressed an internal report that urged a review of ValuJet three months before one of the low-cost carrier's jets crashed in Florida's Everglades, an FAA manager testified on Friday.

A public hearing into the cause of the crash of ValuJet Flight 592 ended with a pledge from victims' families to fight for improved air safety standards and a vow from investigators to increase protections for the travelling public.

A stunned audience heard testimony from FAA management that the agency was aware of serious problems with ValuJet's maintenance procedures but the information was deliberately kept secret from regional inspectors.

Some relatives of the 110 people who died when the DC-9 plunged into the Everglades on May 11 blamed "corporate greed" for the oversight that allowed volatile oxygen canisters, suspected of fuelling a fire in the cargo hold, to be carried on the plane.

"A tragedy that should not have happened, happened. It happened because of corporate greed ... and a government that appears to put the material things of life over the more important things, which are human relationships," said Richard Kessler of Atlanta, whose wife, Kathy, died in the crash.

On the final day of a week-long National Transportation Safety Board hearing into the crash, FAA manager John Tutora, who worked at the Washington Air Carrier Branch, said he had expressed serious concerns about ValuJet in February -- three months before the disaster.
Tutora said he had written a detailed report in which he concluded the airline was "ill" but his senior management told him to keep the findings "confidential."

FAA officials conceded for the first time that they ordered their investigation simply because Congress and the Inspector General were carrying out their own inquiries into ValuJet's safety standards.
NTSB hearing chairman John Goglia criticised Tutora for failing to follow up his report by ensuring that senior management had evaluated his recommendations.
"This smells. It really smells, when you have a report that was done in preparation for investigational hearings," Goglia said.

However, Tutora claimed he did not feel his position allowed him to take his report any further. Later, a senior FAA official, William White, said he had not even seen the report until after the crash.
White, FAA deputy director of flight standards, said the agency was understaffed and often unable to deal with its workload, in particular with the rapid expansion of ValuJet.
"Because of the astonishing growth that took place, the system failed," he said.
Investigators heard testimony that FAA inspectors were unable to keep up with routine paperwork or properly inspect ValuJet's maintenance contractors.

The five-day hearing traced a series of critical errors that allowed dozens of oxygen canisters to be improperly packed and loaded into the DC-9's cargo hold, where they may have sparked or fuelled a ferocious fire that sent toxic smoke throughout the aircraft.
The NTSB was not expected to rule on the cause of the crash for several months.
